pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Plant-Eaters vs Meat-Eaters (ages 5–7): sort dinosaurs into herbivores (plant-eaters) and carnivores (meat-eaters) by reading clues on the animal itself — especially TOOTH SHAPE: flat/blunt teeth grind plants, sharp/pointed teeth tear meat.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify and describe carnivores, herbivores and omnivores) — this is the direct statutory anchor, applied to dinosaurs; supports 'working scientifically' (identify and classify using observable features).
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports K–2 life-science patterns/observation; no dino-specific PE, but classification-by-evidence underpins grade-3 fossil reasoning.
• Operational details — The key move is CLASSIFY-WITH-REASON: children don't just label, they justify from a visible clue. Teach the tooth rule (sharp points = cut meat; flat ridges = grind tough plants) and support with other clues (long neck for reaching leaves; claws for grabbing prey). This seeds 'form fits diet' — evidence-based inference, the domain's spine — at a concrete level. Note some dinosaurs were plant-eaters despite being huge and scary-looking (size ≠ carnivore). Keep to two categories (skip omnivores here unless a child raises it).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): sorts a dinosaur as plant-eater or meat-eater with adult prompting. Tier B (~6): uses the tooth clue to justify a sort ('sharp teeth → meat'). Tier C (~7): independently sorts several dinosaurs and explains the tooth (and one other) clue for each.
bestPractices: Make TEETH the primary observable clue and always ask 'how do you know?' so sorting is reasoned, not guessed — this seeds evidence-based inference.
Zoom in on real tooth shapes: serrated points (steak-knife) for meat vs flat/leaf-shaped grinders for plants.
Add corroborating clues (long neck to reach foliage, grasping claws) so children learn multiple features point the same way.
Bust 'big & scary = meat-eater': show a giant gentle long-neck plant-eater to break the size–diet link.
Connect to the Y1 herbivore/carnivore vocabulary children already meet with living animals, transferring the idea to dinosaurs.
keyRepresentations: Close-up tooth cards: sharp serrated points vs flat ridged grinders, paired with 'meat' / 'plants'.
A two-bin sorter: plant-eater vs meat-eater, with a 'clue' popup on each drop.
Whole-animal clue overlays (teeth + neck + claws) that all point to the same diet.
A 'detective' frame: examine the clue, then decide.
commonMisconceptions: 'Big or fierce-looking dinosaurs must be meat-eaters' — the largest dinosaurs were plant-eating long-necks.
'All dinosaurs ate meat' (fed by scary media) — most known dinosaurs were herbivores.
'You can tell diet from size/colour' — the reliable clue is teeth (and jaws), not size.
'Sharp teeth always mean it hunted big animals' — sharp teeth mean meat/flesh, but could be fish or small prey.
'Plant-eaters have no defences' — many had horns, plates, or spikes despite eating plants.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, children classify dinosaurs as plant-eaters (herbivores) or meat-eaters (carnivores) by reading a visible clue on the animal — especially tooth shape (sharp, often serrated blades or points for slicing and tearing flesh; blunt, peg-like, leaf-shaped or flat ridged teeth for stripping, shredding or grinding plants). The core move is classify-WITH-REASON: not just labelling but justifying from an observed feature, with corroborating clues (long neck for reaching foliage; sharp hooked claws on many meat-eaters, though claws alone are not proof because some plant-eaters had big claws too) and a deliberate challenge to the 'big/scary = meat-eater' misconception, since some of the largest dinosaurs were plant-eaters.

activities.title: Tooth detective: sort and justify
feedback: When a sort is correct, play back the child's reasoning: 'Blunt, flat teeth strip or grind tough leaves — plant-eater!' or 'Sharp points cut flesh — meat-eater!'

If the child calls the giant long-neck a meat-eater because it is biggest, redirect to the teeth: the biggest long-necked dinosaurs had blunt peg- or spoon-shaped teeth for stripping leaves (not sharp meat-cutting blades) and ate plants; size does not decide diet.
If the child reverses the rule (sharp = plant, flat = meat), match the action to the shape: tearing meat needs sharp points, while stripping or grinding leaves is done with blunt or flat teeth.
If the child says all dinosaurs ate meat, point out that most known dinosaurs were plant-eaters and name a clear herbivore example.

When the giant plant-eater is revealed, you can add that many plant-eaters still had defences such as horns, plates, or spikes even though they ate plants — so being well-armed does not mean it hunted; the teeth still tell you the diet.
activities.rationale: Classification is reasoned from an observable feature rather than guessed, which seeds evidence-based inference ('form fits diet'). The zoom/magnify tool, two-bin drop, reasoning playback, agreeing second clue, an optional free-explore mode to inspect any tooth before deciding, and the giant-herbivore trap case are concrete interaction examples that make the learning mechanism visible; they are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Tooth shape indicates diet: carnivorous dinosaurs had sharp, often serrated teeth for cutting flesh, while herbivores had flatter, ridged or leaf-shaped teeth for grinding/stripping plants; the largest dinosaurs (sauropods) were herbivores.
learnerActions: Examine a dinosaur's teeth close-up (zoom/magnify a tooth image): decide whether they are sharp, serrated meat-cutting points or blunt plant-eating teeth (pegs, leaf shapes or flat grinding ridges).
Place the dinosaur into a PLANT-EATER bin or a MEAT-EATER bin.
Say out loud or record WHY: 'blunt or flat teeth strip or grind leaves, so plant-eater' / 'sharp points tear meat, so meat-eater'.

After a correct sort, look at a second clue (long neck for reaching branches, or sharp hooked claws) and check whether it points to the same diet — remembering that claws are only a hint, because some plant-eaters had big claws too.
Optionally use a free-explore mode to flip open and inspect any dinosaur's tooth close-up before committing to a bin.
Meet a 'trap' case: a colossal long-necked dinosaur that looks fierce but has blunt peg-like teeth for stripping leaves (not sharp blades) — decide its diet from the teeth, not its size.
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape is usually a good clue to diet, and multiple body features can agree; a dinosaur's size or scary appearance does NOT decide what it ate — evidence over first impression.

activities.title: Tooth-rule poster to read first
feedback: Confirm the match between tooth shape and diet when the child reads it correctly.
If the child only memorises labels without reasons, prompt: 'What is that tooth shape good for doing?'
activities.rationale: A clear contrasting reference teaches the rule explicitly and is useful as a lead-in or reminder. On its own it does not require the child to perform the sort-and-justify, so it works best alongside the active sorting task rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Tooth shape indicates diet: carnivorous dinosaurs had sharp, often serrated teeth for cutting flesh, while herbivores had flatter, ridged or leaf-shaped teeth for grinding/stripping plants; the largest dinosaurs (sauropods) were herbivores.
learnerActions: Study a contrast display of a sharp serrated (steak-knife) tooth beside a flat ridged grinder, each labelled with 'meat' or 'plants'.
Tap or point to example dinosaurs to see which group they belong to and the reason why.
State the rule back in your own words before attempting the sorting activity.
activities.intendedInsight: Sharp pointed teeth are for cutting/tearing meat; flat ridged teeth are for grinding plants — a clear rule to apply when sorting.

activities.title: Check the concept: categorise and choose
feedback: If a diet is assigned by size or fierceness, restate that teeth, not size, reveal diet.
If the child cannot name examples, supply a clear herbivore and a clear carnivore to anchor the categories.
activities.rationale: A short categorisation plus a targeted question verifies whether the tooth–diet link holds and whether the child can give examples. This checks understanding; it does not by itself elicit the independent reason-giving that building the detective inference requires, so use it after the active sorting rather than as the main teaching.
sourceClaims: UK Y1 science requires identifying and describing carnivores, herbivores and omnivores — the classification foundation applied here to dinosaurs.
learnerActions: Sort a set of about four dinosaurs into herbivore and carnivore groups.
Answer: 'Sharp pointed teeth are for…?' (choose: tearing meat / grinding plants).
Name one plant-eating dinosaur and one meat-eating dinosaur.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can apply the tooth rule and give examples of each diet group.

activities.title: Fossil-detective talk (optional Socratic variant)
feedback: Acknowledge reasoning that cites tooth shape; gently probe when diet is inferred from size.
Offer the giant plant-eater as a counter-case if the child ties size to meat-eating.
activities.rationale: A guided dialogue can draw out the child's reasoning and address misconceptions in the moment. For this age a hands-on, self-paced sorter is often easier to sustain than open dialogue, so this is offered as a complementary option rather than the primary route.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'What do the teeth tell you about what this dinosaur ate?'
Explain your reasoning aloud and respond to a follow-up: 'Does being big mean it ate meat?'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the tooth clue in conversation reinforces reasoning from evidence rather than appearance.

constraints: Keep to two categories (plant-eater / meat-eater); introduce omnivores only if a child raises it.

Teeth (and jaws) are the primary clue; corroborate with other features (neck, claws) so children see multiple features agreeing, noting that claws are a weaker clue because some plant-eaters also had large claws.
Always ask 'how do you know?' so sorting is reasoned, not guessed.
Deliberately include at least one giant plant-eater to break the 'big/scary = meat-eater' link.
A contrast poster or reference image teaches the rule but does not itself require the child to perform the sort-and-justify; pair it with active sorting.
A categorisation/multiple-choice check verifies the concept but does not by itself elicit the independent reason-giving that building the inference requires.
Sharp teeth indicate a meat/flesh diet but not necessarily hunting of large prey — prey could be fish or small animals; avoid overstating.
Note that plant-eaters could still be well-defended (horns, plates, spikes); defences and size do not signal a meat diet — the teeth do.
Connect to Year 1 herbivore/carnivore vocabulary children already meet with living animals, transferring the idea to dinosaurs.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim about tooth shape and the largest dinosaurs (sauropods) being herbivores is attributed to museum education pages but is unverified here; present the tooth-diet rule as a reliable clue for this age level, not an exhaustive scientific account.

The legacy entry asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a quiz/poster only verifies rather than builds reasoning. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (a reference image can still teach; a check can be used during teaching).
Original framing stated the misconception is 'directly' broken and the insight lands 'with a jolt'; retained as a design aim, not an evidence claim of effectiveness.

probeDeeper: Brachiosaurus was one of the biggest dinosaurs ever — did it eat meat or plants? How do you know?
Why would sharp pointed teeth be no good for eating tough leaves all day?
Name one plant-eating dinosaur and one meat-eating dinosaur.
assess.correctAnswer: The huge long-necked one with flat blunt teeth ate PLANTS (flat teeth grind leaves) — even though it's the biggest. The smaller one with sharp pointed teeth ate MEAT (sharp teeth tear flesh). You tell from tooth shape, not size: being big does NOT mean a dinosaur was a meat-eater — some of the biggest dinosaurs were plant-eaters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Big or scary-looking dinosaurs ate meat — the giant one must be a carnivore.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to teeth: the biggest sauropods had blunt grinding teeth and ate plants; size doesn't decide diet.
errorPatterns.distractor: The huge one ate meat because it's the biggest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns diet by size; calls the huge long-necked one a meat-eater.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the tooth–diet link — sharp teeth for plants, flat teeth for meat.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match the action to the shape: tearing meat needs points, grinding leaves needs flat surfaces.
errorPatterns.distractor: Flat teeth are for tearing meat and sharp teeth are for plants.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Swaps which tooth shape goes with which diet.

errorPatterns.pattern: All dinosaurs ate meat / were fierce hunters.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that most dinosaurs were herbivores; give clear plant-eater examples.

responseLevels.gap: Assigns diet by size or fierceness, or reverses the tooth–diet link.
responseLevels.full: Reads diet from tooth shape, holds that size doesn't determine diet (big plant-eaters exist), and gives a herbivore and a carnivore example.
responseLevels.partial: Links tooth shape to diet in a clear case but slips when size and diet conflict (a big herbivore).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two dinosaurs: one is huge with a long neck and small flat, blunt teeth; the other is smaller with a big head full of sharp pointed teeth. Which one ate plants and which ate meat? How can you tell from the teeth — and does being BIG mean a dinosaur ate meat?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads diet from size or fierceness calls the giant one a meat-eater. A child who reads tooth shape gets it right and holds that size is irrelevant to diet. The tier-two 'does being big mean it ate meat' directly separates the two.
